newsitem.title: USA: Oil prices fall sharply, soybeans rise, on weather.
newsitem.headline: Oil prices fall sharply, soybeans rise, on weather.

text.p: Oil prices went into a tailspin Monday after forecasts of higher temperatures in the Northeast triggered a sell-off in heating oil.

"Prices started to break down as soon as forecasts for warmer weather came out. Heating oil then led us down most of the day," said Ed Kevelson, director of refined products for Paribas Futures Inc. in New York.
On the New York Mercantile Exchange, February heating oil closed down 2.45 cents a gallon at 69.70 cents.
After a frigid start to 1997, forecasts for the Northeast, the world's largest heating oil market, pointed to more normal temperatures this week.

Charlie Notis, meteorologist with Freese-Notis Weather in Des Moines, Iowa, said temperatures would rise to normal levels Tuesday through Thursday before a cold snap sends the mercury to 8 to 10 degrees below normal over the weekend.

By late next week, a cold air mass will move across the Midwest into the Northeast, but the cold front will be weaker than the one the Northeast experienced last weekend, said meteorologist Jon Davis of brokerage Smith Barney in Chicago.
European and U.S. heating oil stocks have been on a steady rise in recent weeks, further easing concerns about supplies.
Pressured by heating oil's sharp drop, February crude oil closed down 90 cents a barrel at $25.19, and February gasoline dropped 2.27 cents a gallon to 68.09 cents.
Despite Monday's weakness, traders were not yet ready to say February crude has peaked after hitting a contract high of $26.74 a barrel Thursday.

"One day does not make a trend," said William Brown of trading firm W.H. Brown & Co. "But in the next couple of weeks we should know whether crude has entered a higher trading range set in 1996 or if its going back to $18."
At the Chicago Board of Trade, soybean prices posted three-month highs as the market was boosted for a second straight session by worries about hot weather in South America and smaller U.S. stocks.
January soybeans peaked at $7.38 per bushel early Monday, topping the high of $7.37 set Oct. 11. The contract closed at $7.32-3/4, up 6 cents.
Growers in Brazil, the leading U.S. competitor as a soybean exporter, said some areas in the key Rio Grande do Sul region remained without rain and were starting to suffer.
"There's not much relief in sight in southern Brazil and the stocks are tight, the tightest stocks-to-usage ratio in about 20 years," said Vic Lespinasse of Dean Witter Reynolds.

On Friday, soybeans soared the 30-cent per bushel daily trading limit after the Agriculture Department said 1996 U.S. soybean production was 2.382 billion bushels, below average trader estimates of 2.407 billion.
The government also cut its estimate for end-of-season soybean stockpiles on Sept. 1, 1997, to 155 million bushels, below its previous forecast of 180 million.

Wheat futures closed higher, with March wheat up 4 cents a bushel at $3.91. Traders cited worries about the effect of freezing temperatures and winds on the dormant winter wheat crop in the Midwest and Plains states.
"The acreage number was a very low number. Also, the cold weather in the Plains is causing concern," said Ron Kucha of O'Connor and Co.
The Agriculture Department on Friday said U.S. farmers last fall seeded only 48.2 million acres of winter wheat, well below an average analyst estimate of 51.4 million acres.
